//! Band-limited delta resampling. The source clock is the NTSC CPU clock;
//! the output clock is 44.1 kHz. Keeping the clock fraction avoids frame drift.
const CPU_HZ: u64 = 1_789_773;
const CLOCK_SCALE: u64 = CPU_HZ * 12;
const PHASES: usize = 256;
const TAPS: usize = 34;
pub struct Resampler {
    kernels: Vec<[f64; TAPS]>,
    ring: [f64; 128],
    head: usize,
    integrator: f64,
    last: f64,
    phase: u64,
    emitted: u64,
    started: bool,
    hp1_x: f64,
    hp1_y: f64,
    hp2_x: f64,
    hp2_y: f64,
    lp: f64,
}
impl Resampler {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        let mut kernels = vec![[0.0;TAPS];PHASES+1];
        for (p, kernel) in kernels.iter_mut().enumerate() {
            let frac = p as f64 / PHASES as f64;
            let mut sum = 0.0;
            for (i, k) in kernel.iter_mut().enumerate() {
                let x = i as f64 - 16.0 - frac;
                let w =
                    if x.abs() < 16.0 {
                        0.42 + 0.5 * (std::f64::consts::PI * x / 16.0).cos() +
                            0.08 * (2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI * x / 16.0).cos()
                    } else { 0.0 };
                let z = std::f64::consts::PI * x * 0.9206;
                *k =
                    if z.abs() < 1e-12 {
                        0.9206 * w
                    } else { 0.9206 * w * z.sin() / z };
                sum += *k;
            }
            for k in kernel { *k /= sum; }
        }
        Self {
            kernels,
            ring: [0.0; 128],
            head: 0,
            integrator: 0.0,
            last: 0.0,
            phase: 8 * 44100 * 12,
            emitted: 0,
            started: false,
            hp1_x: 0.0,
            hp1_y: 0.0,
            hp2_x: 0.0,
            hp2_y: 0.0,
            lp: 0.0,
        }
    }
    pub fn clock(&mut self, level: f64) -> Option<i16> {
        let delta = level - self.last;
        if delta != 0.0 {
            self.last = level;
            let clock =
                (self.phase + 44100 * 12) as f64 / CLOCK_SCALE as f64 -
                    (8.0 * 44100.0 * 12.0 / CLOCK_SCALE as f64);
            let center =
                17.0 + clock - if self.started { 1.334 } else { 0.0 };
            self.started = true;
            let base = center.floor() as isize - 16;
            let pos = (center - center.floor()) * PHASES as f64;
            let p = pos as usize;
            let f = pos - p as f64;
            for i in 0..TAPS {
                let offset = base + i as isize;
                if offset >= 0 {
                    let k =
                        self.kernels[p][i] +
                            f * (self.kernels[p + 1][i] - self.kernels[p][i]);
                    self.ring[(self.head + offset as usize) & 127] += delta * k;
                }
            }
        }
        self.phase += 44100 * 12;
        if self.phase < CLOCK_SCALE { return None }
        self.phase -= CLOCK_SCALE;
        self.integrator += self.ring[self.head];
        self.ring[self.head] = 0.0;
        self.head = (self.head + 1) & 127;
        self.emitted += 1;
        if self.emitted <= 17 { return None }
        let x = self.integrator;
        let y = 0.987259035 * self.hp1_y + 0.987259035 * (x - self.hp1_x);
        self.hp1_x = x;
        self.hp1_y = y;
        let z = 0.939235180 * self.hp2_y + 0.939235180 * (y - self.hp2_x);
        self.hp2_x = y;
        self.hp2_y = z;

# APU Sweep

> Source: <https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/APU_Sweep> — NESdev Wiki, revision [24338](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?oldid=24338) (last edited 2026-10-02T00:47:49Z), retrieved 2026-10-06. Authors: NESdev Wiki contributors ([history](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?title=APU_Sweep&action=history)). Images omitted. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md) for license.

An [NES APU](APU.md) sweep unit can be made to periodically adjust a [pulse channel](APU_Pulse.md)'s period up or down.

## Sweep registers ($4001 / $4005, write)

* $4001 corresponds to [Pulse 1](APU_Pulse.md#Sweep_control_($4001_/_$4005,_write))'s sweep unit
* $4005 corresponds to [Pulse 2](APU_Pulse.md#Sweep_control_($4001_/_$4005,_write))'s sweep unit

```
7  bit  0
---- ----
EPPP NSSS
|||| ||||
|||| |+++- Bit shift count
|||| +---- Negate flag
||||           0: add to period, sweeping toward lower frequencies
||||           1: subtract from period, sweeping toward higher frequencies
|+++------ Clock counter divider value
+--------- Enable flag
```

Writing to this register also sets reload flag.

## Updating the period

When the [frame counter](APU_Frame_Counter.md) generates a half-frame clock (at 120 or 96 Hz), two things occur:

1. If the clock divider's counter *is* zero, the sweep is enabled (via [E flag](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))), the shift count ([S bits](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))) is nonzero,
   1. and the sweep unit is *not* [muting](#Muting) the channel: the pulse's period is set to the target period.
   2. and the sweep unit *is* [muting](#Muting) the channel: the pulse's period remains *unchanged*, but the sweep unit's divider continues to count down and reload the divider's period as normal.
2. If the clock divider's counter *is* zero *or* the reload flag is true: The divider counter is set to P and the reload flag is cleared. Otherwise, the divider counter is decremented.

If the sweep unit is disabled including because the shift count is zero, the pulse channel's period is never updated, but muting logic still applies.

## Calculating the target period

The sweep unit continuously calculates each pulse channel's **target period** in this way:

1. A barrel shifter shifts the pulse channel's 11-bit [raw timer period](APU_Pulse.md) right by the shift count ([S bits](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))), producing the change amount.
2. If the negate flag ([N bit](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))) is true, the change amount is made negative.
3. The target period is the sum of the current period and the change amount, clamped to zero if this sum is negative.

For example, if the negate flag ([N bit](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))) is false and the shift count ([S bits](#Sweep_registers_($4001_/_$4005,_write))) is zero, the change amount equals the current period, making the target period equal to *twice* the current period.

The two pulse channels have their adders' carry inputs wired differently, which produces different results when each channel's change amount is made negative:

* Pulse 1 adds the [ones' complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ones%27_complement) (*−c − 1*). Making 20 negative produces a change amount of −21.
* Pulse 2 adds the [two's complement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two%27s_complement) (*−c*). Making 20 negative produces a change amount of −20.

Whenever the current period or sweep setting changes, whether by [$400x](APU_Pulse.md#Registers) writes or by sweep updating the period, the target period also changes.

    pub fn write_reg(&mut self, c: &mut Cart, reg: u16, val: u8, cycle: u64) {
        self.bus_set(val, 255);
        let r = reg & 7;
        if cycle < 29658 && [0, 1, 5, 6].contains(&r) { return }
        #[cfg(feature="trace")]
        if r == 1 {

62:The three unimplemented bits of each sprite's byte 2 do not exist in the PPU and always read back as 0 on PPU revisions that allow reading PPU OAM through [OAMDATA](PPU_registers.md#OAMDATA) ($2004). This can be emulated by ANDing byte 2 with $E3 either when writing to or when reading from OAM. Bits that have decayed also read back as 0 through OAMDATA. These are side effects of the DRAM controller precharging an internal data bus with 0 to prevent writing high-impedance values to OAM DRAM cells.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Writing N to this register causes the DMA circuitry inside the 2A03/07 to fully initialize the OAM by writing [OAMDATA](PPU_registers.md#OAMDATA) 256 times using successive bytes from starting at address $100*N). # PPU sprite evaluation

> Source: <https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/PPU_sprite_evaluation> — NESdev Wiki, revision [22442](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?oldid=22442) (last edited 2025-02-11T12:50:14Z), retrieved 2026-10-06. Authors: NESdev Wiki contributors ([history](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?title=PPU_sprite_evaluation&action=history)). Images omitted. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md) for license.

**PPU sprite evaluation** is an operation done by the PPU once each scanline. It prepares the set of sprites and fetches their data to be rendered on the next scanline.

This is a separate step from sprite rendering.

## Overview

Each scanline, the PPU reads the spritelist (that is, Object Attribute Memory) to see which to draw:

1. First, it clears the list of sprites to draw.
2. Second, it reads through OAM, checking which sprites will be on this scanline. It chooses the first eight it finds that do.
3. Third, if eight sprites were found, it checks (in a wrongly-implemented fashion) for further sprites on the scanline to see if the sprite overflow flag should be set.
4. Fourth, using the details for the eight (or fewer) sprites chosen, it determines which pixels each has on the scanline and where to draw them.

## Details

During all visible scanlines, the PPU scans through OAM to determine which sprites to render on the next scanline. Sprites found to be within range are copied into the secondary OAM, which is then used to initialize eight internal sprite output units.

*OAM[n][m]* below refers to the byte at offset *4*n + m* within OAM, i.e. OAM byte *m* (0-3) of sprite *n* (0-63).

During each pixel clock (341 total per scanline), the PPU accesses OAM in the following pattern:

1. Cycles 1-64: Secondary OAM (32-byte buffer for current sprites on scanline) is initialized to $FF - attempting to read $2004 will return $FF. Internally, the clear operation is implemented by reading from the OAM and writing into the secondary OAM as usual, only a signal is active that makes the read always return $FF.
2. Cycles 65-256: Sprite evaluation
   * *On odd cycles, data is read from (primary) OAM*
   * *On even cycles, data is written to secondary OAM (unless secondary OAM is full, in which case it will read the value in secondary OAM instead)*
   * 1. Starting at n = 0, read a sprite's Y-coordinate (OAM[n][0], copying it to the next open slot in secondary OAM (unless 8 sprites have been found, in which case the write is ignored).
     * 1a. If Y-coordinate is in range, copy remaining bytes of sprite data (OAM[n][1] thru OAM[n][3]) into secondary OAM.
   * 2. Increment n
     * 2a. If n has overflowed back to zero (all 64 sprites evaluated), go to 4
     * 2b. If less than 8 sprites have been found, go to 1
     * 2c. If exactly 8 sprites have been found, disable writes to secondary OAM because it is full. This causes sprites in back to drop out.
   * 3. Starting at m = 0, evaluate OAM[n][m] as a Y-coordinate.
     * 3a. If the value is in range, set the sprite overflow flag in $2002 and read the next 3 entries of OAM (incrementing 'm' after each byte and incrementing 'n' when 'm' overflows); if m = 3, increment n
     * 3b. If the value is not in range, increment n **and** m (without carry). If n overflows to 0, go to 4; otherwise go to 3
       * *The m increment is a hardware bug - if only n was incremented, the overflow flag would be set whenever more than 8 sprites were present on the same scanline, as expected.*
   * 4. Attempt (and fail) to copy OAM[n][0] into the next free slot in secondary OAM, and increment n (repeat until HBLANK is reached)
3. Cycles 257-320: Sprite fetches (8 sprites total, 8 cycles per sprite)
   * 1-4: Read the Y-coordinate, tile number, attributes, and X-coordinate of the selected sprite from secondary OAM
   * 5-8: Read the X-coordinate of the selected sprite from secondary OAM 4 times (while the PPU fetches the sprite tile data)

## assistant · 00:33:55

The sprite mismatch came from OAM address tracking. Turning rendering off during sprite evaluation leaves the hardware address partway through a sprite; the next DMA starts there. Tracking that address fixes the missing frame, and Robot Finds Kitten now matches all 5,000 frames of the varied replay.

    fn publishing_a_prepared_pixel_does_not_advance_sprite_zero_or_the_clock() {
        let mut ppu = Ppu::new();
        ppu.dot = 2;
        ppu.mask = 0x1e;
        ppu.lo = 0xffff;
        ppu.pal[17] = 42;
        ppu.count = 1;
        ppu.sprites[0] = Sprite { x: 0, attr: 0, lo: 128, hi: 0, index: 0 };
        let phase = (ppu.frame, ppu.scan, ppu.dot, ppu.ticks);
        ppu.publish_next_pixel();
        assert_eq!(ppu.fb[1], 42);
        assert_eq!((ppu.frame, ppu.scan, ppu.dot, ppu.ticks), phase);
        assert_eq!(ppu.status & 64, 0);
        assert_eq!(ppu.sprites[0].lo, 128);
        assert_eq!(ppu.lo, 0xffff);

        let mut rom = vec![0; 16 + 16384];
        rom[..4].copy_from_slice(b"NES\x1a");
        rom[4] = 1;
        let mut cart = Cart::load(&rom).unwrap();
        ppu.tick(&mut cart);
        assert_eq!(ppu.fb[1], 42);
        assert_eq!(ppu.status & 64, 64);
        assert_eq!(ppu.sprites[0].lo, 0);
    }
}

diagnostics 30 unexpected []
# APU Frame Counter

> Source: <https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/APU_Frame_Counter> — NESdev Wiki, revision [23448](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?oldid=23448) (last edited 2026-01-19T03:49:39Z), retrieved 2026-10-06. Authors: NESdev Wiki contributors ([history](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?title=APU_Frame_Counter&action=history)). Images omitted. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md) for license.

The **[NES APU](APU.md) frame counter** (or **frame sequencer**) generates low-frequency clocks for the channels and an optional 60 Hz interrupt.
The name "frame counter" might be slightly misleading because the clocks have nothing to do with the video signal.

The frame counter contains the following: [divider](APU.md#Glossary), looping clock [sequencer](APU.md#Glossary), frame interrupt flag.

The sequencer is clocked on every other CPU cycle, so 2 CPU cycles = 1 APU cycle. The sequencer keeps track of how many APU cycles have elapsed in total, and each step of the sequence will occur once that total has reached the indicated amount (with an additional delay of one CPU cycle for the quarter and half frame signals). Once the last step has executed, the count resets to 0 on the next APU cycle.

<table>
<tr><td>Address</td><td>Bitfield</td><td>Description</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>$4017</b></td><td><tt>MI--.----</tt></td><td><b>Set mode and interrupt</b> (write)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Bit 7</td><td><tt>M--- ----</tt></td><td>Sequencer mode: 0 selects 4-step sequence, 1 selects 5-step sequence</td></tr>
<tr><td>Bit 6</td><td><tt>-I-- ----</tt></td><td>Interrupt inhibit flag. If set, the frame interrupt flag is cleared, otherwise it is unaffected.</td></tr>
<tr><td colspan="2">Side effects</td><td>After 3 or 4 CPU clock cycles*, the timer is reset.<br/>If the mode flag is set, then both "quarter frame" and "half frame" signals are also generated.</td></tr></table>

* If the write occurs *during* an APU cycle, the effects occur 3 CPU cycles after the **$4017** write cycle, and if the write occurs *between* APU cycles, the effects occurs 4 CPU cycles after the write cycle.

PAL behavior is currently assumed to be the same.

The frame interrupt flag is connected to the [CPU](CPU.md)'s [IRQ](IRQ.md) line. It is set at a particular point in the 4-step sequence (see below) provided the interrupt inhibit flag in $4017 is clear, and can be cleared either by reading $4015 (which also returns its old status) or by setting the interrupt inhibit flag.

### Mode 0: 4-Step Sequence (bit 7 of $4017 clear)

<table>
<tr><th rowspan="2">Step</th><th colspan="2">APU cycles</th><th rowspan="2"><a href="APU_Envelope.md">Envelopes</a> &amp; <a href="APU_Triangle.md">triangle's linear counter</a><br/>(Quarter frame)</th><th rowspan="2"><a href="APU_Length_Counter.md">Length counters</a> &amp; <a href="APU_Sweep.md">sweep units</a><br/>(Half frame)</th><th rowspan="2">Frame interrupt flag</th></tr>
<tr><th>NTSC</th><th>PAL</th></tr>
<tr><td>1</td><td>3728, PUT</td><td>4156, PUT</td><td>Clock</td><td> </td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>2</td><td>7456, PUT</td><td>8313, PUT</td><td>Clock</td><td>Clock</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>3</td><td>11185, PUT</td><td>12469, PUT</td><td>Clock</td><td> </td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td rowspan="3">4</td><td>14914, GET</td><td>16626, GET</td><td> </td><td> </td><td>Set if interrupt inhibit is clear</td></tr>
<tr><td>14914, PUT</td><td>16626, PUT</td><td>Clock</td><td>Clock</td><td>Set if interrupt inhibit is clear</td></tr>
<tr><td>0 (14915), GET</td><td>0 (16627), GET</td><td> </td><td> </td><td>Set if interrupt inhibit is clear</td></tr>

fn impulse(x: f64) -> f64 {
    if x.abs() >= 16.0 { return 0.0; }
    let position = (x + 18.0) * 64.0;
    let i = position.floor() as usize;
    let t = position - i as f64;
    let t2 = t * t;
    let t3 = t2 * t;
    let weights = [
        (1.0 - t).powi(3) / 6.0,
        (3.0 * t3 - 6.0 * t2 + 4.0) / 6.0,
        (-3.0 * t3 + 3.0 * t2 + 3.0 * t + 1.0) / 6.0,
        t3 / 6.0,
    ];
    let mut result = 0.0;
    for j in 0..4 { result += IMPULSE_COEFFS[i + j] * weights[j]; }
    result
}
''')

# NES emulator

Rust NES emulator for the offline ABI in `spec/ABI.md`.

```
cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
```

The output is `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/nes_emu.wasm`. It exports
all ten ABI functions and linear memory, and requires no host imports.

The CPU implements all official and unofficial opcodes, with individual bus
accesses, DMA, and interrupt polling. CPU instructions are Rust futures that
suspend between bus cycles; the scheduler drives the PPU three dots and the
APU one cycle per CPU bus cycle. The PPU uses background shifters, secondary
OAM evaluation, sprite fetches, scrolling registers, and palette indices.
Cartridges support NROM, MMC1, UxROM, CNROM, and MMC3, including CHR RAM,
MMC1 outer PRG banking, MMC3 bank inversion and IRQs, and NES 2.0 RAM sizes.
Audio uses the five APU channels, nonlinear mixing, fractional-clock
band-limited resampling, and high/low-pass filters.

The implementation is under active development and is not fully accurate.
The bundled oracle is the compatibility target. Its first `run_frame` call
returns the initialized framebuffer without executing CPU cycles; this was
verified with a ROM that samples a button at its first instructions. The
frame wrapper completes its current CPU instruction, and the framebuffer
is updated in place, matching the oracle's observable top-row behavior.
DMA transfers suspend at a frame boundary and resume on the next call.

## Development tools

The native runner writes palette-index frames and raw little-endian i16 audio.
Set `LAST_ONLY=1` to save only the final image. The wasm checker uploads a ROM
into the exported buffer, runs input and frame calls in wasmtime, checks audio
draining, and prints framebuffer/audio FNV hashes, sample count, and rate.
It uses a separate WAT harness and does not add imports to the emulator.

The assembly probes in `tools/` are original diagnostic ROMs. They isolate
startup input, DAC transitions, and individual audio channels. Their linker
configuration is `tools/nrom.cfg`. The optional `trace` feature logs CPU/APU
writes and mixer transitions for native debugging.

//! the output clock is 44.1 kHz. Keeping the clock fraction avoids frame drift.
const CPU_HZ: u64 = 1_789_773;

    hp2_x: f64,

   Compiling nes_emu v0.1.0 (/task)

"""Measure reference DAC-marker write times by exact synthetic CPU replays.

Given a native trace containing WRITE <cycle> 4011 <value> and the oracle
WAV for that diagnostic ROM, replay every DAC write at several cycle offsets.
The closest local waveform identifies the reference timestamp without making
assumptions about its resampler. Reports transitions whose reference phase is
covered by the requested offset range; inspect RMSE before trusting a match.
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import json
import pathlib
import subprocess
import sys
import wave
import numpy as np

p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
p.add_argument('trace')
p.add_argument('reference')
p.add_argument('frames', type=int)
p.add_argument('output')
p.add_argument('--radius', type=int, default=5)
a = p.parse_args()
out = pathlib.Path(a.output)
out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def read_wav(path):
    with wave.open(str(path)) as w:
        assert w.getframerate() == 44100 and w.getnchannels() == 1
        return np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()), '<i2').astype(float)


reference = read_wav(a.reference)
candidates = []
signature = dict(trace=hashlib.sha256(pathlib.Path(a.trace).read_bytes()).hexdigest(),
                 frames=a.frames,
                 builder=hashlib.sha256(pathlib.Path('tools/replay_noise.py').read_bytes()).hexdigest())
cache_file = out / 'input.json'
cache_valid = cache_file.exists() and json.loads(cache_file.read_text()) == signature
offsets = list(range(-a.radius, a.radius + 1))
for offset in offsets:
    rom = out / f'replay_{offset}.nes'
    wav = out / f'replay_{offset}.wav'
    if not cache_valid or not wav.exists():
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, 'tools/replay_noise.py', a.trace,
                        str(rom), '--registers', '4011,4017', '--offset',
                        str(offset)], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL)
        subprocess.run(['oracle', 'run', str(rom), str(a.frames),
                        '--dump-audio', str(wav)], check=True,
                       stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    candidates.append(read_wav(wav))
cache_file.write_text(json.dumps(signature, indent=2))

last = 0
results = []
for line in pathlib.Path(a.trace).read_text().splitlines():
    row = line.split()
    if row[:1] != ['WRITE'] or row[2] != '4011':
        continue
    cycle, value = int(row[1]), int(row[3]) & 127
    if value == last:
        continue
    last = value
    center = int(cycle * 44100 / 1789773 - 1.334)
    low, high = center - 5, center + 20
    if low < 0 or high >= min(len(reference), *(len(c) for c in candidates)):
        continue
    scores = [float(np.sqrt(np.mean((c[low:high] - reference[low:high]) ** 2)))
              for c in candidates]
    index = int(np.argmin(scores))
    result = dict(native_cycle=cycle, reference_cycle=cycle + offsets[index],
                  offset=offsets[index], value=value, rmse=scores[index])
    results.append(result)
    print(json.dumps(result), flush=True)
(out / 'timing.json').write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2))
```

"""Infer individual oracle DAC-marker times, then verify with a CPU replay.

Use an original marker ROM which leaves triangle at its power DAC and uses
only $4011 for sound. This fits individual CPU cycles with the generic FIR;
verify inferred timestamps by an oracle DAC-only replay, not by fit error.
"""

from scipy.signal import lfilter
from scipy.interpolate import BSpline
p=argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__);p.add_argument('trace');p.add_argument('wav');p.add_argument('output');p.add_argument('--radius',type=int,default=8);a=p.parse_args()
with wave.open(a.wav) as w:pcm=np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()),'<i2').astype(float)
r=44100/1789773;r1=np.exp(-2*np.pi*90/44100);r2=np.exp(-2*np.pi*440/44100);alpha=1-np.exp(-2*np.pi*14000/44100)
u=lfilter([1,alpha-1],[alpha],pcm+np.sign(pcm)*.5);u=lfilter([1,-r2],[r2,-r2],u);u=lfilter([1,-r1],[r1,-r1],u);u=np.diff(u,prepend=0)
s=pathlib.Path('src/audio_kernel.rs').read_text();s=s[s.index('= [')+3:s.index('];')];coeff=np.array([float(x) for x in re.findall(r'[-+]?\d+\.\d+e[-+]\d+',s)]);knots=np.r_[[-18]*3,np.arange(-18,18+1/512,1/256),[18]*3];spline=BSpline(knots,coeff,3)
rows=[];previous=0;original=pathlib.Path(a.trace).read_text().splitlines()
def mix(v):return 32767*163.67/(24329/(45+v)+100)
for line in original:
 w=line.split()
 if w[:1]==['WRITE'] and w[2]=='4011':
  t,v=int(w[1]),int(w[3])&127;delta=mix(v)-mix(previous);previous=v
  if delta and 32<(t-8)*r<len(pcm)-50:rows.append((t,v,delta))
choices=np.arange(-a.radius,a.radius+1);models=[];slices=[];selection=np.full(len(rows),a.radius,dtype=int);pred=np.zeros(len(u))
for i,(t,v,delta) in enumerate(rows):
 ts=(t+choices-8)*r;quant=np.floor((ts+8*r)*256)/256-(ts+8*r)+1/512
 ids=np.floor((t-8)*r).astype(int)+np.arange(-19,21);x=ids[None,:]-ts[:,None]-quant[:,None]+1.30936
 kernels=spline(np.clip(x,-18,18));kernels[np.abs(x)>=16]=0;kernels/=kernels.sum(axis=1)[:,None];kernels*=delta
 models.append(kernels);slices.append(ids);pred[ids]+=kernels[a.radius]
residual=u-pred
for iteration in range(12):
 changes=0
 for i,kernels in enumerate(models):
  ids=slices[i];old=selection[i];without=residual[ids]+kernels[old];scores=np.sum((kernels-without[None,:])**2,axis=1);new=int(scores.argmin())
  if new!=old:residual[ids]+=kernels[old]-kernels[new];selection[i]=new;changes+=1
 print('iteration',iteration,'changed',changes,flush=True)
 if not changes:break
shifted={t:t+int(choices[j]) for (t,v,d),j in zip(rows,selection)};output=[]
for line in original:
 w=line.split()
 if w[:1]==['WRITE'] and w[2]=='4011' and int(w[1]) in shifted:w[1]=str(shifted[int(w[1])]);line=' '.join(w)
 output.append(line)
pathlib.Path(a.output).write_text('\n'.join(output)+'\n')
print('offset counts',np.unique(choices[selection],return_counts=True),'events',len(rows),flush=True)

42-* CPU $6000-$7FFF: 8 KB PRG-RAM bank, (optional)
43-* CPU $8000-$BFFF: 16 KB PRG-ROM bank, either switchable or fixed to the first bank
44-* CPU $C000-$FFFF: 16 KB PRG-ROM bank, either fixed to the last bank or switchable
45-* PPU $0000-$0FFF: 4 KB switchable CHR bank
46-* PPU $1000-$1FFF: 4 KB switchable CHR bank

49-
50-## Interface
51-
52-Unlike almost all other mappers, the MMC1 is configured through a serial port in order to reduce its pin count. CPU $8000-$FFFF is connected to a common shift register.
53-Writing a value with bit 7 set ($80 through $FF) to any address in $8000-$FFFF clears the shift register to its initial state.
54-To change a register's value, the CPU writes five times with bit 7 clear and one bit of the desired value in bit 0 (starting with the low bit of the value).
55-On the first four writes, the MMC1 shifts bit 0 into a shift register.
56-On the fifth write, the MMC1 copies bit 0 and the shift register contents into an internal register selected by bits 14 and 13 of the address, and then it clears the shift register.
57-Only on the fifth write does the address matter, and even then, only bits 14 and 13 of the address matter because the mapper doesn't see the lower address bits (similar to the mirroring seen with [PPU registers](PPU_registers.md)). RAM_READ trace rows record the CPU read time and next PPU dot. The probe

from scipy.interpolate import BSpline

rows=[list(map(int,l.split()[1:])) for l in pathlib.Path(a.trace).read_text().splitlines() if l.startswith('RAM_READ ')]

with wave.open(a.wav) as w:pcm=np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()),'<i2').astype(float)
r=44100/1789773;ts=(t-8)*r;valid=ts<len(pcm)-20;rows=rows[valid];t=t[valid];ts=ts[valid];scan=scan[valid];dot=dot[valid]

q=np.floor((ts+8*r)*256)/256-(ts+8*r)+1/512;ids=np.floor(ts).astype(int)[:,None]+np.arange(-19,20)[None,:];x=ids-ts[:,None]-q[:,None]+1.30936
k=f(np.clip(x,-18,18));k[np.abs(x)>=16]=0;k/=k.sum(axis=1)[:,None];flat=ids.ravel();n=len(pcm)
r1=np.exp(-2*np.pi*90/44100);r2=np.exp(-2*np.pi*440/44100);alpha=1-np.exp(-2*np.pi*14000/44100);den=np.convolve(np.convolve([1,-r1],[1,-r2]),[1,alpha-1]);num=np.array([1,-1])*r1*r2*alpha

 stream=np.bincount(flat,weights=(delta[:,None]*k).ravel(),minlength=n)[:n]
 return np.trunc(boot+lfilter(num,den,stream))
native=sound(rows[:,4]);print('prediction from actual native reads',np.sqrt(np.mean((native-pcm)**2)),flush=True)
results=[]
for nt,bg,sp,pre,zero,early in itertools.product(range(3),range(4,8),range(2,5),range(4,8),[False,True],[False,True]):

 value=np.where(pin[scan,dot],34,17);pred=sound(value);err=pred-pcm;rms=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(err*err)));results.append((rms,nt,bg,sp,pre,zero,early,int(np.max(np.abs(err)))))

            }
        }
    }
    let mut audio = Vec::new();
    for frame in 0..frames {
        for &(f, k) in &changes { if f == frame { n.set_keys(k) } }

        for &p in &n.bus.borrow().ppu.fb {

        }

            if self.irq_counter == 0 || self.irq_reload {
                self.irq_counter = self.irq_latch
            } else { self.irq_counter -= 1 }
            self.irq_reload = false;
            if self.irq_counter == 0 && self.irq_enable { self.irq = true }
        }
        self.a12 = high;
    }
}

First recover a spline from inverse-filtered impulses, holding out half the
input phases. Then refine in PCM space so quantization noise is not amplified
by the inverse filters. Validate generated coefficients with fresh patterns
and game replays before adopting them.

"""Build an original NROM diagnostic that replays timestamped APU writes.

The default register set isolates noise. --registers 4011,4017 replays DAC
markers, and --offset permits measuring reference write timing in CPU cycles.
Every generated instruction and branch-page penalty is accounted for.
"""
import argparse
import pathlib

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
parser.add_argument('trace')
parser.add_argument('rom')
parser.add_argument('--registers', default='400c,400e,400f,4015,4017')
parser.add_argument('--max-cycles', type=int, default=20_000_000)
parser.add_argument('--offset', type=int, default=0)
args = parser.parse_args()
registers = {int(a, 16) for a in args.registers.split(',')}
rows = []
for line in pathlib.Path(args.trace).read_text().splitlines():
    if not line.startswith('WRITE '):
        continue
    _, cycle, addr, value = line.split()
    cycle, addr, value = int(cycle), int(addr, 16), int(value)
    if addr in registers and cycle < args.max_cycles:
        rows.append((cycle + (args.offset if cycle > 10000 else 0), addr, value))

code = bytearray([0x78])  # SEI; first fetch follows the eight reset cycles.
clock = 10
accumulator = None


def emit(data, cycles):
    global clock
    code.extend(data)
    clock += cycles


def delay(n):
    # A nested Y/X loop gives long delays without filling the 32 KiB PRG.
    while n > 2000:
        if (len(code) & 255) > 245:
            emit([0xea], 2)
            n -= 2
            continue
        count = min(255, (n - 1) // 1281)
        if n - (1281 * count + 1) == 1:
            count -= 1
        if not count:
            break
        cost = 1281 * count + 1
        emit([0xa0, count, 0xa2, 255, 0xca, 0xd0, 0xfd, 0x88, 0xd0, 0xf8], cost)
        n -= cost
    while n > 3:
        if n >= 6 and (len(code) & 255) in [251, 252, 253]:
            emit([0x24, 0], 3)
            n -= 3
            continue
        count = min(255, (n - 1) // 5)
        if count == 0:
            break
        cost = 5 * count + 1
        if n - cost == 1:
            count -= 1
            cost = 5 * count + 1
        if count == 0:
            break
        emit([0xa2, count, 0xca, 0xd0, 0xfd], cost)
        n -= cost
    while n >= 2:
        if n & 1:
            emit([0x24, 0], 3)
            n -= 3
        else:
            emit([0xea], 2)
            n -= 2
    assert n == 0, n


initialized = False
for target, addr, value in rows:
    if target > 10000 and not initialized:
        # A zero-page value lookup gives a three-cycle load when a two-cycle
        # immediate load would leave an impossible one-cycle delay.
        for v in range(256):
            emit([0xa9, v, 0x85, v], 5)
        accumulator = 255
        initialized = True
    load = [] if accumulator == value else [0xa9, value]
    required = 4 + (2 if load else 0)
    left = target - clock - required
    if left == 1:
        assert initialized
        load = [0xa5, value]
        required = 7
        left = target - clock - required
    assert left >= 0, (target, clock)
    delay(left)
    if load:
        emit(load, 3 if load[0] == 0xa5 else 2)
        accumulator = value
    emit([0x8d, addr & 255, addr >> 8], 4)
    assert clock == target
assert len(code) < 32762, len(code)
end = 0x8000 + len(code)
emit([0x4c, end & 255, end >> 8], 3)
prg = code + bytes(32762 - len(code)) + bytes([
    end & 255, end >> 8, 0, 0x80, end & 255, end >> 8])
rom = b'NES\x1a' + bytes([2, 0, 0, 0]) + bytes(8) + prg
pathlib.Path(args.rom).write_bytes(rom)
print('bytes', len(code), 'cycles', clock)
bytes 3576 cycles 75035341

## assistant · 02:40:05

The phase probes support a general fix: the reference rounds the scaled fractional phase to single precision before lookup and uses the preceding phase at exact sample boundaries. With that change, the DAC probe’s peak error falls from 77 to 4. In the 5,000-frame replays, Stallar’s peak falls from 10 to 3 and File Fixers’ from 4 to 1; sample counts still match. I’ll rebuild and check the wasm artifact next.

        // Timer/reader requests become visible in this clock before DMA
        // arbitrates the CPU's queued bus operation.
        self.tick();
        let next_cycle = self.cycles;
        let get_cycle = next_cycle & 1 == 0;
        let cpu_read = matches!(op, CycleOp::Read(_));
        let was_halted = self.oam_active || self.dmc_active;
        let mut oam_started = false;
        let mut dmc_started = false;
        if !self.apu.dmc_need() && !self.dmc_active {
            self.dmc_pending_at = None;
        }
        if cpu_read {
            if let Some(page) = self.dma.take() {
                self.oam_active = true;
                self.oam_page = page;
                self.oam_index = 0;
                self.oam_have_data = false;
                oam_started = true;
            }
            if !self.dmc_active && self.dmc_pending_at.is_some_and(|t| t <= next_cycle) {
                self.dmc_pending_at = None;

197:Using sprite overflow is often a last resort. When mapper IRQs are not available, the [DMC IRQ](APU_DMC.md#Usage_of_DMC_for_syncing_to_video) can be an effective alternative for timing, albeit complicated to use.
392:If currently playing DPCM samples, there is a chance that an interruption from the APU's sample fetch will cause an extra read cycle if it happened at the same time as an instruction that reads $2007. This will cause an extra increment and a byte to be skipped over, resulting in the wrong data being read. See: [APU DMC](APU_DMC.md#Conflict_with_controller_and_PPU_read)
5:The 2A03 contains a pair of DMA units, one for copying sprite data to PPU [OAM](PPU_OAM.md) and the other for copying DPCM sample data to the APU's [DMC](APU_DMC.md) sample buffer. DMA is required for DPCM playback, and it is difficult to fill OAM without DMA. Unfortunately, DMC DMA can also result in data loss when reading registers with side effects, such as the joypads.
9:* The CPU alternates between cycles on which DMA can get (read) and cycles on which DMA can put (write). These are the first and second halves of APU cycles, respectively. At power-on, whether the first CPU cycle is get or put is random.
11:* DMA can only halt on CPU read cycles. On write cycles, the halt fails and the DMA unit tries again next CPU cycle, repeating until successful.
12:* OAM DMA halts the CPU, performs an optional alignment cycle, and then gets and puts 256 times, taking 513 or 514 cycles. It attempts to halt on the first CPU cycle after the $4014 write.
13:* DMC DMA halts the CPU, performs a dummy cycle and an optional alignment cycle, and then gets once, taking 3 or 4 cycles.
14:* The first, "load" DMC DMA after the $4015 write attempts to halt on the get cycle during the 2nd following APU cycle. The other, "reload" DMC DMAs attempt to halt on a put cycle. Failed halts try again on the next CPU cycle, repeating until successful.
17:* DMC DMA can [corrupt joypad and PPUDATA ($2007) reads and cause extraneous reads of $4015-4017](#Register_conflicts).
21:The DMA units cannot just read or write on any cycle as they wish. Instead, they alternate between **get** cycles where they can read and **put** cycles where they can write. If they need to perform an action that is not permitted on the current cycle, they wait.
27:During the DMA process, the CPU is halted and the 2A03's address and data lines are used for data transfer. The process involves a combination of no-operation cycles and access cycles. No-operation cycles come in 3 equivalent types: the halt cycle, a DMC-only dummy cycle, and an optional alignment cycle.
29:When DMA is scheduled, the associated DMA unit attempts to halt the CPU. The CPU only allows this on read cycles. If the CPU is writing, it ignores the halt and the DMA unit waits until the next cycle to try again, repeating until successful. Delays of up to 3 cycles are possible, with read-modify-write instructions having 2 consecutive writes and interrupts having 3. The halting process itself takes 1 CPU cycle, during which no useful work is done.
31:Once the CPU is halted, the DMA unit may need to perform some amount of non-access setup, taking up to 2 cycles. The exact timing of when DMA is scheduled and what kind of setup it needs depends on the type of DMA.
33:The CPU is halted using its internal RDY input. When RDY is deasserted, the 6502 core repeats the last read cycle indefinitely, making no forward progress nor handling interrupts. On 2A03 CPUs, these repeated reads are externally visible on any no-operation DMA cycle, causing data loss if reading a register with side effects. On 2A07 CPUs, it is suspected that a differ

109:## Conflict with controller and PPU read
110-
111-On the 2A03 CPU used in the NTSC NES and Famicom, if a new sample byte is fetched from memory at the same time the program is reading a register that has read side effects (such as [controllers via $4016 or $4017](Controller_reading.md), [PPU data via $2007](PPU_registers.md#PPUDATA), or [the vblank flag via $2002](PPU_registers.md#PPUSTATUS)), that register will see multiple extra reads that result in data loss or corruption. This is mostly a problem for controllers, and special [controller reading code](Controller_reading_code.md#DPCM_Safety) is necessary to work around this.
112-
113-This problem is fixed on the 2A07 series of PAL CPUs by forcing DMA to halt on the first cycle of an instruction, which fetches an instruction opcode and thus isn't normally reading from registers.
114-
115-See [DMA](DMA.md) for a thorough explanation of how DMA works and [how it conflicts with register reads](DMA.md#Register_conflicts).
116-
117-## Usage of DMC for syncing to video
118-
119-DMC IRQs can be used for timed video operations. The following method was discussed on the forum in 2010.[[3]](#cite_note-3)
120-
121-### Concept
122-
123-The NES hardware only has limited tools for syncing the code with video rendering. The VBlank NMI and sprite 0 hit are the only two reasonably reliable flags that can be used, so only 2 synchronizations per frame can be done easily. In addition, only the VBlank NMI can trigger an interrupt; the sprite 0 hit flag has to be polled, potentially wasting a lot of CPU cycles.
124-
125-However, the DMC channel can hypothetically be used for syncing with video instead of using it for sound. Unfortunately it's a bit complicated, but used correctly, it can function as a crude scanline counter, eliminating the need for an advanced mapper.
126-
127-The DMC's timing is completely separate from the video. The DMC's timer is always running, and samples can only start every 8 clock cycles. However, because the DMC's timer isn't synchronized to the PPU in any way, these 8-clock boundaries occur on different scanlines each frame.
128-
129-Here are the steps to achieve stable timing:
130-
131-* At a fixed point in video rendering (we'll use the start of vblank as an example), a dummy single-byte sample at rate $F is started. Due to a hardware quirk†, the sample needs to be started three times in a row like this:
132-
133-```
134-sei
135-lda #$10
136-sta $4015
137-sta $4015
138-sta $4015
139-cli
140-```
141-
142-* The amount of cycles before a DMC IRQ happens is then measured (either using an actual IRQ, or by polling $4015).
143-  * At rate $F, there are 54 CPU cycles between clocks, so there are 432 CPU cycles (432 × 3 ÷ 341 = about 3.8 scanlines) between boundaries.
144-* The main sample that will be used for the timing is then started (please refer to the table below to have sample lengths for various waiting times)
145-* When the main IRQ happens, the measurement from before is retrieved, and a timing loop with variable delay is used. In order to synchronize with vblank, after a DMC IRQ we should wait 432 CPU cycles minus the time we measured.
146-
147-†**Note:** The hardware quirk mentioned above deals with how DMC IRQs are generated. Basically, the IRQ is generated when the last **byte** of the sample is **read**, **not** when the last *sample* of the sample *plays*. The sample buffer sometimes has enough time to empty itself between writes to $4015, meaning your next write to $4015 will trigger an immediate IRQ. [Fortunately, writing to $4015 three times will avoid this issue.](https://forums.nesdev.org/viewtopic.php?p=66712#p66712)

        assert_eq!(start, 462);
        nes.clock();
        let mut puts = 0;
        while nes.bus.borrow().oam_active {
            let address = nes.bus.borrow().ppu.oam_addr;
            nes.clock();
            let b = nes.bus.borrow();
            if b.ppu.oam_addr != address {
                assert_eq!(b.cycles & 1, 1);
                puts += 1;
            }
        }
        assert_eq!(puts, 256);
        assert_eq!(nes.bus.borrow().cycles - start, 515);
        for i in 0..256 { assert_eq!(nes.bus.borrow().ppu.oam[i], i as u8); }
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_controller_clocks_once_per_contiguous_output_enable() {
        let (nes, _) = fixture(None);
        let mut b = nes.bus.borrow_mut();
        b.keys = 2;
        b.raw_write(0x4016, 1);
        b.raw_write(0x4016, 0);
        assert_eq!(b.raw_read(0x4016) & 1, 0);
        assert_eq!(b.raw_read(0x4016) & 1, 0);
        assert_eq!(b.raw_read(0x4016) & 1, 0);
        b.raw_read(0x8000);
        assert_eq!(b.raw_read(0x4016) & 1, 1);
    }

    #[test]
    fn a_dmc_shadow_read_keeps_the_same_controller_output_enable() {
        let (nes, _) = fixture(None);
        let mut b = nes.bus.borrow_mut();
        b.keys = 2;
        b.raw_write(0x4016, 1);
        b.raw_write(0x4016, 0);
        assert_eq!(b.raw_read(0x4016) & 1, 0);
        b.dma_halt_addr = 0x4016;
        b.cart.prg[0x4816] = 255;

## assistant · 04:16:05

The broader rule matches all 215 collision probes: DMC retains the bus byte from before its transfer, and the next I/O read can perform an extra access when that byte selects the register. This also fixes the false repeats on indexed and mirrored reads. The five dense stream tests now have peak audio error of 2, down from 136–137, and all 38 unit tests pass.

"""Build original DAC impulses immediately below all 256 phase boundaries.

The clock ratio reduces to14700/596591. Modular inversion places each
write at the closest representable CPU cycle below its desired phase.
Long gaps isolate the filter response; this probes numerical phase rules
without relying on a game's APU sequencing or cartridge implementation.
"""
import argparse,math,pathlib,subprocess
p=argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
p.add_argument('prefix');a=p.parse_args()
prefix=pathlib.Path(a.prefix);prefix.parent.mkdir(parents=True,exist_ok=True)
period=596591;inverse=pow(14700,-1,period);last=10000;rows=[];phases=[]
for phase in range(256):
 numerator=phase*period//256
 clock=(numerator*inverse)%period
 clock+=max(0,math.ceil((last+3500-clock)/period))*period
 rows.extend([f'WRITE {clock} 4011 96',f'WRITE {clock+1700} 4011 0'])
 phases.append(f'{phase} {clock}')
 last=clock+1700
trace=prefix.with_suffix('.txt');trace.write_text('\n'.join(rows)+'\n')
prefix.with_suffix('.phases').write_text('\n'.join(phases)+'\n')
subprocess.run(['python3','tools/replay_noise.py',str(trace),str(prefix.with_suffix('.nes')),
 '--registers','4011','--max-cycles',str(last+1)],check=True)
print('frames',math.ceil(last/(1789773/60.0988))+3,'last write',last)

import pathlib,sys,wave,numpy as np
sys.path.insert(0,'tools');from audio_phase import adjustment
r=44100/1789773;r1=.9872590350155737;r2=.9392351762287491
constant=r1*r2/((1-r1)*(1-r2));period=1700*r
f=lambda v:32767*163.67/(24329/(45+v)+100)
def tail(r,a):return r**a*(a*a/(1-r)+2*a*r/(1-r)**2+r*(1+r)/(1-r)**3)
for v in [16,64,96,127]:
 with wave.open(f'.out/filter-mid/dac{v}.wav') as w:pcm=np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()),'<i2').astype(float)
 vals=[];areas=[];first=[]
 for l in pathlib.Path(f'.out/filter-mid/dac{v}.phases').read_text().splitlines():
  p,t=map(int,l.split());center=(t-8)*r-1.334+float(adjustment(t));fall=(t+1700-8)*r-1.334+float(adjustment(t+1700));start=int(np.floor(center))-20
  y=pcm[start:start+800];y+=np.sign(y)*.5;n=np.arange(len(y))+start-center
  valid=(n>=100)&(n<=450)&(abs(y)>4)
  basis=np.c_[r1**n[valid],r2**n[valid]];coeff=np.linalg.lstsq(basis,y[valid],rcond=None)[0]
  cutoff=np.searchsorted(n,400);a=n[cutoff]
  moment=np.sum(n[:cutoff]**2*y[:cutoff])+coeff[0]*tail(r1,a)+coeff[1]*tail(r2,a)
  area=np.sum(y[:cutoff])+coeff[0]*r1**a/(1-r1)+coeff[1]*r2**a/(1-r2)
  fm=np.sum(n[:cutoff]*y[:cutoff])+sum(c*q**a*(a/(1-q)+q/(1-q)**2) for c,q in zip(coeff,[r1,r2]))
  vals.append(moment/(2*constant*(fall-center)));areas.append(area);first.append(fm)
 a=np.array(vals);true=f(v)-f(0);print(v,'gamma',np.mean(a),'true',true,'diff',np.mean(a)-true,'ppm',1e6*(np.mean(a)/true-1),'se',np.std(a)/16,'area',np.mean(areas),'firstmoment',np.mean(first),flush=True)

NES Eval Oracle — black-box reference emulator

The oracle runs a reference NES emulator on any ROM and returns the exact
framebuffer and audio output. Use it to compare your emulator's output
against the reference and iterate until they match.

COMMANDS:

  oracle help
      Show this help message.

  oracle info
      Print JSON with frames used so far, framebuffer format, resolution
      and audio format.

  oracle run <rom> <frames> [options]
      Power on the reference with <rom> (state per spec/ABI.md) and run it
      for <frames> frames. Prints a JSON summary to stdout.

      Options:
        --replay <file>       Feed a recorded input sequence (format below)
        --dump-frames <dir>   Write every frame as <dir>/frame_NNNNN.ppm (RGB
                              image) and <dir>/frame_NNNNN.idx (raw palette
                              indices, the bytes emu_framebuffer() must hold)
        --dump-final <dir>    Write only the last frame, same two files
        --dump-audio <file>   Write the audio as a mono 16-bit WAV, 44100 Hz
        --from <n>            --dump-frames and --dump-audio cover frames >= n
                              only (the emulator still runs from power-on)

  oracle session ...
      Stateful, ABI-shaped API: start a ROM, set keys, run frames, read the
      framebuffer and audio. Run `oracle session help` for details (task
      container only; provided by its oracle client).

EXAMPLES:

  # What does the reference draw in the first second of a game?
  oracle run dev-roms/<game>.nes 60 --dump-frames /tmp/ref

  # Compare your frame 59 with the reference, byte for byte
  cmp /tmp/ref/frame_00059.idx my_frame_59.idx

  # Run with inputs and capture audio
  oracle run dev-roms/<game>.nes 600 --replay my-inputs.txt --dump-audio /tmp/ref.wav

FRAMES:
  Frame N is the frame completed by the (N+1)-th emu_run_frame() call after
  emu_load_rom(); the keys for frame N are set with emu_set_keys() before
  that call.

PIXEL FORMAT:
  256x240. .idx files: 61440 little-endian u16 values, row-major, each
  (emphasis << 6) | colour, as emu_framebuffer() in spec/ABI.md. PPM files
  are the same frame mapped to RGB through spec/nes_palette.pal.

AUDIO FORMAT:
  Mono signed 16-bit at 44100 Hz, as emu_audio_buffer() in spec/ABI.md
  (about 735 samples per frame).

REPLAY FORMAT:
  Text, one line per change: `<frame> <keys_hex>`. Keys are active-high:
  bit 0=A, 1=B, 2=Select, 3=Start, 4=Up, 5=Down, 6=Left, 7=Right.
  The keys stay held until the next line. `#` starts a comment.

USAGE:
  `oracle info` shows how many frames you have run so far. There is no
  limit; use the oracle as much as you need.

spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/Errata.md:56:<li>On C, E, G and H PPUs, when rendering begins automatically on pre-render dot 0, the address changes from OAM1ADDR to OAM2ADDR mid-access and reliably copies the OAM1ADDR row to the OAM2ADDR row, regardless of alignment. This does not appear to be capable of analog corruption of the OAM2ADDR row and does not occur on letterless, A, B, or D PPUs.</li></ul></td><td>
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/PPU_registers.md:225:OAMADDR is set to 0 during each of ticks 257–320 (the sprite tile loading interval) of the pre-render and visible scanlines. This also means that at the end of a normal complete rendered frame, OAMADDR will always have returned to 0.
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/PPU_registers.md:254:* Writes to OAMDATA during rendering (on the pre-render line and the visible lines 0–239, provided either sprite or background rendering is enabled) do not modify values in OAM, but do perform a glitchy increment of [OAMADDR](#OAMADDR), bumping only the high 6 bits (i.e., it bumps the *[n]* value in [PPU sprite evaluation](PPU_sprite_evaluation.md) – it's plausible that it could bump the low bits instead depending on the current status of sprite evaluation). This extends to DMA transfers via [OAMDMA](#OAMDMA), since that uses writes to $2004. For emulation purposes, it is probably best to completely ignore writes during rendering.
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/PPU_sprite_evaluation.md:77:* Sprite evaluation does not happen on the pre-render scanline. Because evaluation applies to the next line's sprite rendering, no sprites will be rendered on the first scanline, and this is why there is a 1 line offset on a sprite's Y coordinate.

//! Band-limited delta resampling. The source clock is the NTSC CPU clock;
//! the output clock is 44.1 kHz. Keeping the clock fraction avoids frame drift.
const CPU_HZ: u64 = 1_789_773;
const CLOCK_SCALE: u64 = CPU_HZ * 12;
const PHASES: usize = 256;
const TAPS: usize = 33;
#[path = "audio_phase_table.rs"]
mod kernel;
pub struct Resampler {
    kernels: Vec<[f64; TAPS]>,
    ring: [f64; 128],
    head: usize,
    integrator: f64,
    last: f64,
    phase: u64,
    emitted: u64,
    started: bool,
    hp1_x: f64,
    hp1_y: f64,
    hp2_x: f64,
    hp2_y: f64,
    lp: f64,
}
impl Resampler {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        let kernels = kernel::TABLES.to_vec();
        Self {
            kernels,
            ring: [0.0; 128],
            head: 0,
            integrator: 0.0,
            last: 0.0,
            phase: 8 * 44100 * 12,
            emitted: 0,
            started: false,
            hp1_x: 0.0,
            hp1_y: 0.0,
            hp2_x: 0.0,
            hp2_y: 0.0,
            lp: 0.0,
        }
    }
    pub fn clock(&mut self, level: f64) -> Option<i16> {
        let delta = level - self.last;
        if delta != 0.0 {
            self.last = level;
            if !self.started {
                // Fixed power-on clock phase. These are the cumulative taps
                // of the startup impulse after the 17-sample output delay.
                const STARTUP: [f64; 17] = [
                    0.938755072726, 1.031980775353, 0.984252702826,
                    1.006131841473, 0.999401487416, 0.997925765493,
                    1.002991013871, 0.997121668659, 1.002222053117,
                    0.998539525466, 1.000865880595, 0.999587988277,
                    1.000071909274, 0.999928906261, 0.999984257325,
                    1.000027795906, 1.0,
                ];
                let mut previous = 0.0;
                for (i, &cumulative) in STARTUP.iter().enumerate() {
                    self.ring[(self.head + 17 + i) & 127] +=
                        delta * (cumulative - previous);
                    previous = cumulative;
                }
                self.started = true;
            } else {
                // Quantize before removing the reset cycles. The table
                // lookup rounds its scaled fractional phase to f32 first;
                // this matters at representable cycles just below a phase
                // boundary. At an exact whole sample the reference's clock
                // conversion approaches from below, selecting phase255 of
                // the preceding sample. Original 256-phase DAC probes
                // protect both numerical edge cases independently of APU.
                let quantized = Self::quantized_phase(self.phase);
                let p = if self.phase == 0 {255} else {(quantized*256.0) as usize};
                let base = if self.phase == 0 {-1isize} else {0isize};
                for i in 0..TAPS {
                    let offset = base + i as isize;
                    if offset >= 0 {
                        self.ring[(self.head + offset as usize) & 127] += delta * self.kernels[p][i];
                    }
                }
            }
        }

49-
50-## Interface
51-
52-Unlike almost all other mappers, the MMC1 is configured through a serial port in order to reduce its pin count. CPU $8000-$FFFF is connected to a common shift register.
53:Writing a value with bit 7 set ($80 through $FF) to any address in $8000-$FFFF clears the shift register to its initial state.
54:To change a register's value, the CPU writes five times with bit 7 clear and one bit of the desired value in bit 0 (starting with the low bit of the value).
55-On the first four writes, the MMC1 shifts bit 0 into a shift register.
56-On the fifth write, the MMC1 copies bit 0 and the shift register contents into an internal register selected by bits 14 and 13 of the address, and then it clears the shift register.
57:Only on the fifth write does the address matter, and even then, only bits 14 and 13 of the address matter because the mapper doesn't see the lower address bits (similar to the mirroring seen with [PPU registers](PPU_registers.md)). After the fifth write, the shift register is cleared automatically, so writing again with bit 7 set to clear the shift register is not needed.

125:When the serial port is written to on consecutive cycles, it ignores every write after the first. In practice, this only happens when the CPU executes read-modify-write instructions, which first write the original value before writing the modified one on the next cycle.[[2]](#cite_note-2) This restriction only applies to the data being written on bit 0; the bit 7 reset is never ignored. *Bill & Ted's Excellent Adventure* does a reset by using INC on a ROM location containing $FF and requires that the $00 write on the next cycle is ignored. *Shinsenden*, however, uses illegal instruction $7F (RRA abs,X) to set bit 7 on the second write and will crash after selecting the みる (look) option if this reset is ignored.[[3]](#cite_note-3) This write-ignore behavior appears to be intentional and is believed to ignore all consecutive write cycles after the first even if that first write does not target the serial port.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

import pathlib,re,numpy as np
from scipy.signal import lfilter
R1=.9872590350155737;R2=.9392351762287491;ALPHA=.8639403657579068
DEN=np.convolve(np.convolve([1,-R1],[1,-R2]),[1,ALPHA-1])
B=np.array([1,-1])*R1*R2*ALPHA
def level(p,t):return (95.52/(8128/p+100) if p else 0)+(163.67/(24329/t+100) if t else 0)
def trace_events(path):
 rows=[]
 for line in pathlib.Path(path).read_text().splitlines():
  if line.startswith('MIX '):
   _,tick,p1,p2,tri,noise,dmc=map(lambda s:int(s) if s!='MIX' else s,line.split())
   rows.append((tick-1,level(p1+p2,3*tri+2*noise+dmc)))
 return rows

def predict(events,table,n):
 imp=np.zeros(n+33);old=events[0][1]
 for t,value in events[1:]:
  head=t*44100//1789773-17;frac=(t*44100%1789773)/1789773
  q=min(int(np.float32(frac*256)),255)
  if frac==0:head-=1;q=255
  for j,k in enumerate(table[q]):
   if 0<=head+j<len(imp):imp[head+j]+=(value-old)*k
  old=value
 src=pathlib.Path('src/audio.rs').read_text();cdf0=np.array([float(x) for x in re.search(r'STARTUP:.*?= \[(.*?)\];',src,re.S).group(1).replace(',',' ').split()])
 cdf=np.r_[cdf0,np.ones(n-len(cdf0))]
 boot=lfilter(np.array([1,-2,1])*R1*R2*ALPHA,DEN,cdf)*events[0][1]
 return (lfilter(B,DEN,imp)[:n]+boot)*32767
PY

 for name,mask,regs in [('pulse1',1,{0x4000,0x4001,0x4002,0x4003}),('pulse2',2,{0x4004,0x4005,0x4006,0x4007}),('triangle',4,{0x4008,0x400a,0x400b}),('noise',8,{0x400c,0x400e,0x400f})]:
  selected=[]
  for row in rows:
   addr=int(row[2],16)
   if addr==0x4015:row=row.copy();row[3]=str(int(row[3])&mask)
   if addr in regs|{0x4015,0x4017}:selected.append(' '.join(row))
  trace=root/(f's{seed}-'+name+'.txt');trace.write_text('\n'.join(selected)+'\n');rom=trace.with_suffix('.nes');wav=trace.with_suffix('.wav')

  n=np.fromfile(native/'audio.raw','<i2').astype(float)

# APU Length Counter

> Source: <https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/APU_Length_Counter> — NESdev Wiki, revision [24331](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?oldid=24331) (last edited 2026-09-30T00:46:59Z), retrieved 2026-10-06. Authors: NESdev Wiki contributors ([history](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?title=APU_Length_Counter&action=history)). Images omitted. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md) for license.

The length counter provides automatic duration control for the [NES APU](APU.md) waveform channels. Once loaded with a value, it can optionally count down (when the length counter halt flag is clear). Once it reaches zero, the corresponding channel is silenced.

## Clocking

When the [enabled](APU.md#Status_($4015)) bit is cleared (via **$4015**), the length counter is forced to 0 and cannot be changed until enabled is set again (the length counter's previous value is lost). There is no immediate effect when enabled is set.

test='''    #[test]
    fn triangle_length_reload_reaches_the_gate_after_a_coincident_timer_edge() {
        // Original seeded streams restore a stopped triangle exactly one
        //clock before its divider expires. The reference skips that edge,
        //loads the new divider, then advances after the whole new period.
        let mut tri = Triangle::default();
        tri.enable = true;
        tri.linear = 16;
        tri.seq = 24;
        tri.period = 2;
        tri.timer = 0;
        tri.write(3,215);

        tri.timer();
        assert_eq!(tri.output(),8);
        assert!(tri.length>0);
        for _ in 0..1794 { tri.timer(); }
        assert_eq!(tri.output(),8);
        tri.timer();
        assert_eq!(tri.output(),9);
    }
''';assert anchor in s;s=s.replace(anchor,test+anchor);open(p,'w').write(s)

1-# APU Frame Counter
2-
3:> Source: <https://www.nesdev.org/wiki/APU_Frame_Counter> — NESdev Wiki, revision [23448](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?oldid=23448) (last edited 2026-01-19T03:49:39Z), retrieved 2026-10-06. Authors: NESdev Wiki contributors ([history](https://www.nesdev.org/w/index.php?title=APU_Frame_Counter&action=history)). Images omitted. See [SOURCES.md](../SOURCES.md) for license.
4-
5:The **[NES APU](APU.md) frame counter** (or **frame sequencer**) generates low-frequency clocks for the channels and an optional 60 Hz interrupt.
6:The name "frame counter" might be slightly misleading because the clocks have nothing to do with the video signal.
7-
8:The frame counter contains the following: [divider](APU.md#Glossary), looping clock [sequencer](APU.md#Glossary), frame interrupt flag.
9-
10:The sequencer is clocked on every other CPU cycle, so 2 CPU cycles = 1 APU cycle. The sequencer keeps track of how many APU cycles have elapsed in total, and each step of the sequence will occur once that total has reached the indicated amount (with an additional delay of one CPU cycle for the quarter and half frame signals). Once the last step has executed, the count resets to 0 on the next APU cycle.
11-
12-<table>
13-<tr><td>Address</td><td>Bitfield</td><td>Description</td></tr>
14:<tr><td><b>$4017</b></td><td><tt>MI--.----</tt></td><td><b>Set mode and interrupt</b> (write)</td></tr>
15-<tr><td>Bit 7</td><td><tt>M--- ----</tt></td><td>Sequencer mode: 0 selects 4-step sequence, 1 selects 5-step sequence</td></tr>
16-<tr><td>Bit 6</td><td><tt>-I-- ----</tt></td><td>Interrupt inhibit flag. If set, the frame interrupt flag is cleared, otherwise it is unaffected.</td></tr>
17:<tr><td colspan="2">Side effects</td><td>After 3 or 4 CPU clock cycles*, the timer is reset.<br/>If the mode flag is set, then both "quarter frame" and "half frame" signals are also generated.</td></tr></table>
18-
19:* If the write occurs *during* an APU cycle, the effects occur 3 CPU cycles after the **$4017** write cycle, and if the write occurs *between* APU cycles, the effects occurs 4 CPU cycles after the write cycle.

22-

The MMC3 difference came from accepting eight-dot A12-low intervals; the reference requires nine. That change fixes all 48 configurations, and four oracle replays using our IRQ timestamps produce byte-for-byte identical audio. The new DMC random streams found one remaining large audio mismatch, which I’m isolating next.

They are scheduled to halt the CPU on a get cycle during the 2nd APU cycle after the write (that is, the 3rd or 4th CPU cycle). Reload DMAs occur in response to the sample buffer being emptied. Unlike load DMAs, they are scheduled to halt the CPU on a put cycle.
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/DMA.md:121:DMC DMA normally takes 3 or 4 cycles, depending on whether alignment is needed. Because load and reload DMAs schedule on different cycle types, load DMAs take 3 cycles and reload DMAs take 4 unless the halt is delayed by an odd number of cycles. However, bugs can cause additional cycles; see [Bugs](#Bugs) below.

spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/DMA.md:199:DMC DMA suffers from two bugs[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) related to sample playback stopping around the time [a DMC output cycle ends](APU_DMC.md#Output_unit), which is what empties the sample buffer and triggers a reload DMA. This can happen explicitly, where the sample is stopped by clearing $4015 D4, or implicitly, where a non-looping 1-byte sample is started while the sample buffer is empty shortly before a reload DMA would schedule. Implicit stops require this type of sample because the load DMA for the first byte when the sample buffer is empty is the only way to implicitly end the sample just before a reload DMA; longer samples will instead be ended by the reload DMA itself, as normal.
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/DMA.md:201:When sample playback is stopped during the APU cycle before a reload DMA would schedule (that is, on the 2nd or 3rd CPU cycle before the halt attempt), the DMA starts, but is aborted after a single cycle. If the halt is delayed due to a write cycle, the aborted DMA doesn't occur at all. This aborted DMA schedules regardless of how playback was stopped, whether explicitly or implicitly. In the implicit case, the write to begin the sample will normally be the 4th APU cycle before the reload DMA would schedule (8th or 9th CPU cycle before).
spec/docs/nesdev-wiki/DMA.md:203:On RP2A03H and late RP2A03G CPUs, when playback is stopped implicitly on the same APU cycle that a reload DMA would schedule (that is, the 1st CPU cycle before the halt attempt), an unexpected reload DMA occurs from the same address. This extra byte goes into the sample buffer and is played after the first byte, as with any normal fetch. On RP2A03G CPUs, this bug was introduced sometime in 1990; earlier chips are unaffected.

(halted) (get) DMA reads from $xxFF
(halted) (put) DMA writes to $2004       <- DMA completes
         (get) CPU reads from address A  <- CPU resumes execution
```

### DMC DMA

---

DMC DMA copies a single byte to the DMC unit's sample buffer. This occurs automatically after the DMC enable bit, bit 4, of the [sound channel enable register ($4015)](APU.md#Status_($4015)) is set to 1, which starts DPCM sample playback using the current DMC settings in [registers $4010-4013](APU_DMC.md#Overview). DMC DMA is scheduled when all of DPCM playback is enabled, there are bytes left in the sample, and the sample buffer is empty (see [Memory reader](APU_DMC.md#Memory_reader) and [Output unit](APU_DMC.md#Output_unit)). In the common cases, DMC DMA performs a halt cycle, a dummy cycle, an optional alignment cycle,

    pub fn pc(&self) -> u16 { self.cpu.pc }
    pub fn clock(&mut self) {
        let mut cx = Context::from_waker(Waker::noop());
        if self.pending.is_none() {
            let mut cpu = self.cpu.clone();
            self.pending =
                Some(Box::pin(async move { cpu.step().await; cpu }));
            let result =
                self.pending.as_mut().unwrap().as_mut().poll(&mut cx);
            assert!(result.is_pending());
        }
        if !self.bus.borrow_mut().execute() { return }
        if let Poll::Ready(cpu) =
                self.pending.as_mut().unwrap().as_mut().poll(&mut cx) {
            self.cpu = cpu;
            self.pending = None;
        }
    }
    pub fn run_frame(&mut self) {
        if self.first_frame { self.first_frame = false; return }
        let frame = self.bus.borrow().ppu.frame;
        while self.bus.borrow().ppu.frame == frame ||
            (self.pending.is_some() && !self.bus.borrow().last_dma_cycle) {
            self.clock()
        }
        self.bus.borrow_mut().ppu.publish_next_pixel();
    }
}

        let mut rom = vec![0;16+32768];
        rom[..4].copy_from_slice(b"NES\x1a");
        rom[4]=2;
        let mut code=vec![0x78,0xa9,1,0x8d,0x16,0x40];
        for _ in 0..23{code.extend_from_slice(&[0xa2,255,0xca,0xd0,0xfd]);}
        code.extend(std::iter::repeat_n(0xea,200));
        code.extend_from_slice(&[0xa9,2,0x8d,0x14,0x40]);
        let end=0x8000+code.len() as u16;
        code.extend_from_slice(&[0x4c,end as u8,(end>>8) as u8]);
        rom[16..16+code.len()].copy_from_slice(&code);
        rom[16+32764..16+32766].copy_from_slice(&0x8000u16.to_le_bytes());
        let mut nes=Nes::new(Cart::load(&rom).unwrap());
        for i in 0..256{nes.bus.borrow_mut().ram[512+i]=i as u8;}
        nes.run_frame();
        assert_eq!(nes.bus.borrow().cycles,8);
        nes.run_frame();
        assert!(nes.bus.borrow().oam_active);
        assert_eq!(nes.bus.borrow().ppu.oam[255],0);
        nes.run_frame();
        assert!(!nes.bus.borrow().oam_active);
        assert_eq!(nes.bus.borrow().ppu.oam[255],255);
    }

        if self.dmc_left == 0 { return; }

# Task: Implement a Nintendo Entertainment System Emulator

Build an NES emulator that matches a reference emulator's output — both video and audio — across a suite of real games and test ROMs. The target is a fully cycle-accurate implementation of the NTSC NES (the 2A03 CPU and APU, the 2C02 PPU, and cartridge mappers 0 (NROM), 1 (MMC1), 2 (UxROM), 3 (CNROM) and 4 (MMC3)) that plays arbitrary games end-to-end fully correctly, including handling user input (button presses, directional pad, held inputs) so that games progress past title screens, through menus, and into actual gameplay. Rendering a correct idle frame is not enough; the emulator must produce correct output for any input sequence. Audio and video are both first-class outputs, you should work on both in parallel as both must be accurate and are extremely difficult to implement correctly. The power-on state is not random: it is specified exactly in `spec/ABI.md`, and your emulator must reproduce it. You must continue working towards this goal indefinitely.

A truly correct NES emulator is not achievable — there is always more to fix. If you believe you are done, you are mistaken. Keep working.

## What's in the container

| Path | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `spec/ABI.md` | The interface your wasm must export, including the exact power-on state |
| `spec/nes_palette.pal` | The palette used to turn your framebuffer's palette indices into colours |
| `spec/docs/` | NES hardware reference (start at `spec/docs/index.md`) |
| `dev-roms/` | Example NES ROMs |

Do not attempt to access the internet — the test corpus and grading happen offline against the bundled reference, and pulling code from external sources is not what's being evaluated.

Toolchains available: Rust 1.96 with `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, wasmtime, clang with `wasm-ld`, cmake, cc65 (`ca65`, `ld65`, `da65`) for writing or disassembling 6502 code, python3 with numpy and scipy.

## Tools

**`oracle`** — an NES emulator. You do not have access to the source code. Run `oracle help` to see its interface.

## What you produce

A `.wasm` file implementing the functions in `spec/ABI.md`, built for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` as a cdylib.

## Project layout

Your project must be a Rust cargo project at the **root** of `/task/`:

```
/task/
├── Cargo.toml      # [package] name = "nes_emu"
└── src/
    └── lib.rs      # [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]
```

Required:
- Package name is `nes_emu` (underscore, not dash). The artifact will be `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/nes_emu.wasm`.
- Cargo.toml lives at `/task/Cargo.toml`, **not** in a subdirectory like `/task/nes-emu/Cargo.toml`.
- Do not change the package name or move Cargo.toml once work is underway — external tooling expects a stable artifact path at `target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/nes_emu.wasm`.
- Your cdylib exports the functions in `spec/ABI.md`.

The build is always `cargo build --release --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` run from `/task/` with no `.cargo/config.toml` and no custom `RUSTFLAGS`. Write code that doesn't require those.

## Memory

Wasm linear memory grows on demand at runtime via `memory.grow`. You do not need to statically reserve tens of MB of buffers; allocate with `Vec`/`Box` and let the allocator grow the heap as it needs. Large `static mut` arrays that inflate the initial linear-memory size beyond tens of MB can fail to link.

# NES Emulator Wasm ABI

Export these 10 C-ABI functions, plus `memory`, from a `wasm32-unknown-unknown` cdylib:

```c
int       emu_init(void);           // setup, returns 1/0
uint8_t*  emu_rom_buffer(void);     // ≥8 MiB, stable pointer
int       emu_load_rom(int len);    // parse iNES / NES 2.0 image + power on, returns 1/0
int       emu_reset(void);          // identical state to load_rom (cold boot, not the Reset button)
void      emu_set_keys(uint32_t k); // controller 1, active-high, latched
void      emu_run_frame(void);      // advance one frame
uint16_t* emu_framebuffer(void);    // 256×240 palette indices, see below
int16_t*  emu_audio_buffer(void);   // i16 mono
int       emu_audio_samples(void);  // samples since last call (drains)
int       emu_audio_rate(void);     // must return 44100
```

Key bits (the order the controller shifts them out of `$4016`):
0=A, 1=B, 2=Select, 3=Start, 4=Up, 5=Down, 6=Left, 7=Right.

## Framebuffer

One `uint16_t` per pixel, row-major, 256 wide × 240 tall (all 240 rendered
scanlines, no overscan cropping). Each value is

```
(emphasis << 6) | colour
```

where `colour` is the 6-bit value read from palette RAM for that pixel and
`emphasis` is PPUMASK bits 7–5 shifted down (bit 0 = red, bit 1 = green,
bit 2 = blue). Values above `0x1FF` are masked off. The grader converts
indices to RGB with the fixed table in `spec/nes_palette.pal` (512 entries ×
3 bytes, `R G B`, indexed by the same 9-bit value), so the choice of display
palette never affects the score.

## Frames

`emu_run_frame` advances until the PPU leaves the pre-render scanline (261)
for scanline 0. The framebuffer then holds scanlines 0–239 of the frame just
finished. On odd frames with rendering enabled, the pre-render line is one
dot shorter, as on hardware.

## Power-on state

`emu_load_rom` and `emu_reset` must produce exactly this state, which the
reference uses:

- NTSC 2A03 / 2C02 timing.
- CPU work RAM, PRG-RAM (battery or not), palette RAM, OAM and nametable
  VRAM all zero.
- CPU registers at the first instruction fetch: `A=X=Y=0`, `S=$FD`,
  `P=$24`, `PC` = the reset vector at `$FFFC`.
- At that same moment the PPU is at scanline 0, dot 25 (the reset sequence
  has run with the PPU clocking from scanline 0, dot 0).
- CPU/PPU clock alignment and APU cycle parity are fixed, not randomized.
- PPU warm-up (NES behaviour, not Famicom): for the first 29 658 CPU
  cycles after power-on, writes to `$2000`, `$2001`, `$2005` and `$2006`
  are ignored.

## Audio

Mono, signed 16-bit, 44 100 Hz, full scale at ±32767. Samples are produced
during `emu_run_frame`. `emu_audio_samples` returns how many samples have
been produced since its previous call, and `emu_audio_buffer` then points to
them.

## Mappers

The corpus uses mappers 0 (NROM), 1 (MMC1), 2 (UxROM), 3 (CNROM) and
4 (MMC3). MMC1 and MMC3 boards always have at least 8 KiB of PRG-RAM at
`$6000-$7FFF`, even when an NES 2.0 header declares none; a header that
declares more gets that amount.

## Environment

This will be loaded via wasmtime. No threads, no filesystem, no clock, no
main loop. Every import traps when called.

## Other reference discoveries

- The first `emu_run_frame` executes NO CPU cycles and produces no audio.
  Proven with an original startup-input ROM: keys are changed at frame 1
  before its first instruction runs. Nes.first_frame models that behavior.
- The reference updates one framebuffer in place, then completes a normal
  CPU instruction after the PPU wraps. Its output may include a few pixels
  from the next frame at row zero. Double buffering was substantially worse.
- CPU NMI line sampling is after the FIRST PPU tick of each CPU cycle.
  Vector selection for IRQ/BRK uses current NMI after pushing status.
- PPU status read at scanline 241 dot 1 suppresses the pending vblank set.
- Visible dot 0 must present a CHR address for MMC3 A12; doing so on the
  pre-render line too caused a bundled MMC3 diagnostic failure.
- Noise compatibility: reload the full listed period on the half-rate
  clock, giving e.g. 66 CPU cycles for period index 3 (32), unlike the NES
  hardware table's usual interpretation. Power noise shift 0x4000/timer 1.
- DMC rate index 13 is 84. Its power timer is 422 after eight reset cycles.
  A sample at rate 15 empties the buffer at cycle 809 and changes DAC at 863.
  A shared Bus arbiter now handles DMC/OAM overlap; see below.
- Audio output delay is 17 samples and initial clock phase is eight reset
  cycles. A 20,000-frame clock probe constrained CPU_HZ to 1789773 +/-0.06;
  the rounded 1,789,773 Hz clock prevents long-run sample-count drift.
- OAM DMA can suspend at a frame boundary; last_dma_cycle flags preserve its
  pending CPU operation. This is now implemented in Bus, not Cpu futures.
- Triangle timers clock BEFORE coincident frame-counter gate updates. A
  2400-frame File Fixers replay exposed a permanent phase error at 27.9 sec;
  moving the timer ahead of linear/length clocks fixes it (full RMSE 121 ->
  2.04). Small original start/stop edge probes and a unit protect this.

cat >> PROGRESS.md <<'EOF'

## Accepted frame callback correction (51 units)

The earlier assertion that OAM DMA could pause at the frame boundary was
incorrect. Original mask probes .out/dmc-oam-frame-wrap/oam58600..59000
showed reference finishes 1..4 next-frame rows during an overlapping OAM
transfer. Finishing the pending CPU instruction fixes all five probes;
publish_next_pixel must also handle ALL visible scanlines, not only row0
(the last three probes exposed one missing published pixel each).

More decisively, tools/dma_frame_input_probe.py holds A during frame-call2
and releases before call3. Four OAM transfers at planned59100/59400/59500/
59550 cross the boundary; LDA4016 immediately afterward reads A=1 in the
reference. Old callback reads A=0 (all61440 finalpixels wrong); completing
DMA AND its held CPU instruction matches all four. Original old
.out/dma-boundary.nes 8call input fixture also remains allframes exact.
DMC-only looping mask probe all8 cases now exact, including old15pixels

    pub fn address(&mut self, a: u16, dot: u64) {
        if self.mapper == 1 {
            // SxROM boards reuse the currently selected CHR address lines
            // for PRG ROM/RAM. In 4 KiB mode the PPU chooses the register.
            self.chr_upper = a & 0x1000 != 0;
            return;
        }
        if self.mapper != 4 { return }
        let high = a & 0x1000 != 0;
        if !high {
            if self.a12 { self.low_since = dot }
        // Rapid $2000 table switching can produce an eight-dot low
        // interval; the reference rejects it. Nine dots qualifies, which
        // also preserves the odd pre-render line's first background edge.
        } else if !self.a12 && dot.saturating_sub(self.low_since) >= 9 {
            if self.irq_counter == 0 || self.irq_reload {
                self.irq_counter = self.irq_latch
            } else { self.irq_counter -= 1 }
            self.irq_reload = false;
            if self.irq_counter == 0 && self.irq_enable { self.irq = true }
        }
        self.a12 = high;
    }
}

The picture region is generated by doing memory fetches that fill shift registers, from which a pixel is selected. It is composed of a background region filling the entire screen and smaller sprites that may be placed nearly anywhere on it. In the border and any transparent pixel, the PPU displays the palette index selected by the PPU's EXT input, which is grounded to index 0 in stock consoles.

34:To generate the background in the picture region, the PPU performs memory fetches on dots 321-336 and 1-256 of scanlines 0-239 and 261. Each memory fetch takes 2 dots: on the 1st, the full address is placed onto the PPU's address bus and the low 8 bits are stored into an external address latch, and on the 2nd, the read is performed. Fetches require 2 dots because the same physical pins are used for the data bus and low 8 bits of address, so the address must be latched externally before a read can be done.
36:In each 8-dot window, the PPU performs the 4 memory fetches required to produce 8 pixels, fully occupying the PPU bus. Using the current scroll register, v, to produce the target addresses, the PPU fetches a tile ID from the nametable, attributes data from the attributes table, and the low and then high bitplane of the pattern data for that tile ID. The fetched bytes are stored in internal registers.
38:On every 8th dot in these background fetch regions (the same dot on which the coarse x component of v is incremented), the pattern and attributes data are transferred into registers used for producing pixel data. For the pattern data, these transfers are into the high 8 bits of two 16-bit shift registers. For the attributes data, only 2 bits are transferred and into two 1-bit latches that feed 8-bit shift registers. The concept for both is the same, differing merely because the attributes data is the same for all 8 pixels, negating the need to store 8 copies of it.
